Two to 4 inches long and shaped like an egg, the prickly pear has a coarse, thick
skin that can be yellow, orange, pink, magenta, or red, depending on the variety.
The inedible skin is dotted with tubercles that have small, 
almost invisible spines capable of pricking the skin.
The prickly pear’s flesh is mildly sweet, juicy, and 
fragrant and contains numerous edible, small, 
crunchy seeds.  Like the skin, the flesh can 
range from yellow to dark red.

Varieties
Among the common varieties of pum-
melo available in the United States are
the Chandler, Ichang, Red Shaddock,
Reinking, Tresca, and Webber.
Origin & botanical facts
A native of Malaysia, the pummelo is a
popular fruit in east, southeast, and south
Asia.  It is believed to have been intro-
duced to the West Indies by an English
sea captain named Shaddock, by whose
name this fruit is sometimes called.
Pummelo trees are strictly tropical and
grow only in frost-free regions.  They
achieve heights of 15 to 30 feet, and the
crown of the tree is round.  Like other
citrus trees, they bear fruit for many
decades.   Although the pummelo is not
grown commercially in the United States,
